entries.claim: For persistent spatial contact events inside a firmly held grasp (TACO 119 events, ARCTIC 26), the grasp before the event already holds most of the modelled wrench capability of the grasp after it (median pre→post retention 0.85 on TACO and 0.89 on ARCTIC, median profile cosine 0.97 / 0.96, median relative change of the direction-averaged capability +0.04 / +0.02), which supports reading many of these dense reconfigurations as preserving a wrench-capability proxy for functional grasp capability, under the modelled constraints.
entries.metric: Per event: PRE grasp (frame before the event) versus POST grasp (frame after it), each built from the contact at its own frame in the object frame (no transport). Capability profile = support-function capacity h(u) along 76 shared 6-D force/torque directions (64 random, fixed seed, + 12 signed axes) of a contact-patch model (unit force budget per finger and palm, 8-edge Coulomb cone with mu = 0.5, torque divided by the object size); normalised units, not newtons. Retention pre→post = mean over directions of min(h_pre / h_post, 1): 1 = the PRE grasp already had all of the POST grasp's capability (one-sided). Profile cosine = cosine similarity of the two 76-D profiles (1 = same shape; blind to an overall scale change). Relative change = (Q_post − Q_pre) / Q_pre with Q = mean of the profile (0 = unchanged). Table values are MEDIANS over test-split events; intervals are 95 % percentile intervals of a bootstrap that resamples whole takes (1 000 replicates). Neither direction is 'better': values near 1 (retention, cosine) or 0 (relative change) mean the capability is preserved.

caveats: Wrench capability is a modelled PROXY in normalised units (unit finger budgets, linearised Coulomb friction, torque normalised by object size, mesh centroid as torque origin). Object mass, centre of mass, inertia, hand force limits and friction are unavailable in both datasets; this is not a physical feasibility result and says nothing about why the fingers moved (report section 12).

The values are MEDIANS over events, not a statement about every event: 20 % (TACO) / 23 % (ARCTIC) gain more than 25 % and 8 / 3 events lose more than 25 %; only 34 % / 46 % of events retain at least 0.9. The report's own verdict is 'heterogeneous with a dominant function-preserving pattern' ('Case C with a strong Case-A component').

Retention is one-sided by design: a grasp that shrank scores close to 1 (a release scores exactly 1). Quote it together with the reverse retention (0.91 / 0.89), the cosine or the relative change. The report's phrase 'retains 85–90 % of the post grasp's capability in every direction' is loose: it is a mean over directions of a capped ratio, not a per-direction guarantee.

The 0.85 / 0.89 are specific to the single-hand support-function measure (other wrench components assumed balanced by the other hand / table / tool contact). Under the strict exact-direction measure the median retention is 0.66 [0.33, 0.78] (TACO) / 0.75 [0.11, 0.92] (ARCTIC).

TACO shows a small but systematic gain rather than exactly zero: lower CI bound of the median relative change 0.0037 > 0, mean +0.13 [0.07, 0.21], Q_post > Q_pre in 63 % of events (the report attributes it to a slightly larger post grasp). On ARCTIC the interval of the median straddles zero [−0.09, +0.19].
ARCTIC is small: 26 events from 15 takes; its intervals are wide (retention [0.76, 0.96]).

'Persistent spatial' is a minority class defined by two labelled cuts of the earlier event analysis (amount ratio ≤ 0.3; persistence over ±4 frames ≥ 0.5; firm contact before, after and throughout): 123 (119 analysed) of 1 464 detected TACO test events and 26 of 283 on ARCTIC. The larger persistent mixed class (452 / 131) behaves differently. The claim is about this class, not about post-grasp reconfigurations in general.

Events are short: PRE and POST are 1 frame apart in the median TACO event and 2 in the median ARCTIC event (events.csv post_frame − pre_frame; max 13 / 9), so a 'reconfiguration' is a contact-map jump between nearby frames that then persists.
Reference level: the diagnostic transient (frame-jitter) class has retention 0.90 / 0.94, so the persistent spatial class is only slightly below it.

Correction of the task text: retention and cosine do NOT use a transported pre grasp. Each grasp is evaluated at its own frame in the object frame (wrench_analysis.py: geom_dict(g, 'pre') / geom_dict(g, 'post')). Transport by mesh vertex id is used only for the future-motion directions.
The word 'missed' in the block title rests on another report (hand_contact_predictive_info_report.md lines 24–26: 'least explained'); this study measures no prediction error.
OakInk2 is excluded from this study (no hand geometry in the object frame in its caches).

Stale sentences in the report's Limitations section ('TACO's 100 analysed persistent-spatial events ... 61 takes'; 'ARCTIC ... 26 ... (37 takes)') contradict every table (119 / 73 and 26 / 15). The report's '177 / 37 test takes' are takes with at least one detected event; the fixed test split has 186 / 44 takes.

entries.claim: Events that change the contact amount are associated with a capability change more often than persistent spatial ones: persistent mixed events have a median relative capability change of +0.19 (TACO) / +0.16 (ARCTIC) and 46 % of them gain more than 25 % on both datasets (persistent spatial: 20 % / 23 %), amount-dominant events have a median of +0.73 / +0.14, and the onset and release positive controls go from no modelled capability to a grasp and from a grasp to none.
entries.metric: Same measures as the main entry, by event class of the test split (primary setting): relative change of the direction-averaged support-function capacity Q (0 = unchanged), pre→post retention (1 = PRE grasp already had the POST capability; one-sided), share of events within ±25 % and gaining > 25 %. Medians over events with 95 % take-bootstrap CIs; shares have no CI. Classes: persistent mixed = amount ratio between 0.3 and 0.7, firm contact throughout; amount-dominant = amount ratio ≥ 0.7 (diagnostic); onset / regrasp and release = positive controls; transient = persistence < 0.5 (diagnostic).

caveats: 'More often', not 'always': about half of the persistent mixed events still stay within ±25 % (49 % TACO / 43 % ARCTIC).
The spatial / mixed boundary is a labelled cut of the amount ratio at 0.3; the report says so in its limitations.

The profile cosine barely separates the classes (spatial 0.97 / 0.96 versus mixed 0.95 / 0.95) because a cosine ignores an overall scale change; the separation shows in the relative change, the retention and the shares.

The onset 'relative change' values in the CSV and in the report's Table 1 (about 1e9) are a division by epsilon (Q_pre = 0) and must not be quoted; state the control as 'from 0 to a median Q of 1.20 / 0.78'. Release has retention pre→post = 1 by definition of the one-sided measure, which must not be read as 'release preserves capability'.

The positive controls are close to by-construction (no contact patch at the PRE frame of 69 of 77 / 17 of 19 onset events, none at the POST frame of every release): they show that frames and pipeline line up and that the metric is not flat. The graded response of the mixed and amount-dominant classes is the more informative contrast.
ARCTIC amount-dominant interval is very wide ([0.00, 0.95]); the TACO transient class is a random subsample of 150 of 708 events.
Wrench capability is a modelled proxy in normalised units (see the main entry).

entries.claim: Within the persistent spatial class, a capability change above 25 % is associated with a change of the set of contacting hand parts (palm and five fingers): events that keep the same set, including those in which parts slide by more than 1 cm, stay within ±25 % in 61 of 62 (TACO) and 15 of 15 (ARCTIC) cases; 23 of the 24 TACO and 6 of the 6 ARCTIC events that gain more than 25 % have a newly touching part, and 8 of 8 / 3 of 3 events that lose more than 25 % have a part leaving (counts over the per-event table, not printed in the report). In the report's own table the median absolute relative change is 0.03 (TACO) / 0.07 (ARCTIC) when no part is reconfigured against 0.18–0.25 with one or more reconfigured parts, where 'reconfigured' counts a part that slid more than 1 cm as well as one that appeared or disappeared; for persistent mixed events the same split gives 0.04 / 0.02 against 0.25–0.73.
entries.metric: Hand parts = palm + five fingers (MANO skinning-weight labels). A part is 'stable' if it touches before and after with its patch centroid moving ≤ 1 cm, 'slid' if it moved more, 'appeared' / 'disappeared' if it touches only after / only before. The report's Table 5 groups events by the number of reconfigured parts (slid + appeared + disappeared = 0, 1, ≥ 2) and gives the median pre→post retention (1 = preserved) and the median |relative change| of Q (0 = unchanged); no intervals are given. The finger-set split (same set / part added / part removed only) is a count over events.csv rows made in this evidence pass.

caveats: The report's tabulated split is by the NUMBER OF RECONFIGURED PARTS, which counts a part that slid more than 1 cm as well as one that appeared or disappeared; it is not a pure finger-set split. The finger-set counts (same set / part added / part removed only; 23 of 24, 6 of 6, 8 of 8, 3 of 3, 61 of 62, 15 of 15) were counted in this pass from the per-event table events.csv and are not printed in the report; say so if they are used.

The report's supporting sentence 'the 20 % / 23 % of events gaining > 25 % have 0.5–2.7 fingers appearing' is NOT reproduced by events.csv (mean 1.46 parts appear, range 0–4, on TACO; exactly 1 on ARCTIC). Do not quote it.
'Finger removal' evidence is weaker than 'finger addition': the report discusses additions only; the removal statement rests on the events.csv count (12 TACO / 4 ARCTIC 'removed only' events).

On ARCTIC the retention by number of reconfigured parts is flat for the spatial class (0.90 / 0.91 / 0.88 with only 5 / 6 / 15 events); the gradient is visible in |relative change| and in the mixed class.
On TACO spatial the median |relative change| is not monotone in the number of parts (0.03 / 0.20 / 0.18).
Events that only lose parts have a high one-sided retention although their capability fell; use the relative change for them.
This is an association in observational data under one wrench model, with no intervals in the source table; 'hand part' includes the palm.

With unit budgets per finger, an added finger raises the modelled capability by construction of the model (the report: 'keeping the per-finger limits makes finger additions count'); under a single whole-hand budget the classes move closer (see the sensitivity entry).
entries.claim_as_extracted: Within the persistent spatial and the persistent mixed class, the size of the capability change is associated with hand parts being added or removed rather than sliding in place: with no reconfigured part the median absolute relative change is 0.03 (TACO) / 0.07 (ARCTIC) for spatial events against 0.18–0.25 with one or more reconfigured parts, and 23 of the 24 TACO and 6 of the 6 ARCTIC persistent spatial events that gain more than 25 % have a hand part newly touching the object.
entries.correction_reason: Every number is right, but the sentence attaches 'added or removed rather than sliding in place' to the Table-5 split, and that split counts a slid part as reconfigured, so 0.03 / 0.07 versus 0.18-0.25 contrasts 'nothing moved more than 1 cm' with 'something slid, appeared or disappeared' and cannot separate sliding from adding. The sliding-versus-adding contrast is carried by the finger-set counts from events.csv (same set 61 of 62 / 15 of 15 within ±25 %; my recount: slide-only events 32 of 33 TACO and 10 of 10 ARCTIC within ±25 %). 'Removed' rests only on counts made from events.csv (the report discusses additions). The claim also names the mixed class but quoted no mixed number. Association only: with one unit budget per finger an added finger raises the modelled capability by construction.

entries.claim: The size of the dense contact-map change is only weakly associated with the capability change for persistent spatial events on TACO (Spearman 0.19 with the relative change, −0.27 with the retention, n = 119) and moderately on ARCTIC (0.55 / −0.60, n = 26; no interval is given for these correlations). On TACO this is consistent with the size of the contact change providing little information about the capability change: 33 of the 73 events with a contact change at or above the train median keep |relative change| at or below the train median of 0.13 (45 % [34, 57]). On ARCTIC only 1 of the 11 such events does (9 % [0, 30]; train median 0.09); 5 of the 11 gain more than 25 %.
entries.metric: Spearman rank correlation, over test events of one class and dataset, between the contact-map change ‖C_post − C_pre‖₂ (512-D contact map) and (a) the relative change of Q, (b) the pre→post retention. No interval or p-value is given in the source. Quadrant: among persistent spatial test events whose contact change is at or above the median of the TRAIN persistent spatial events, the share whose |relative change| is at or below the train median; 95 % take-bootstrap CI.

caveats: The source gives no confidence interval or p-value for the Spearman values; ARCTIC's 0.55 rests on 26 events and its quadrant statement on 11 events.

'Small capability change' in the quadrant is a strict cut (|relative change| at or below the train median 0.13 / 0.09), not 'within 25 %'. On ARCTIC, of the 11 large-change events only 5 gain more than 25 % (events.csv); the others change by 0.10–0.25 in magnitude and one is a loss.

Do not quote the report's final-answer sentence '... most of the large-contact-change spatial events (10 of 11), on TACO fewer than half (55 %)': 55 % (40 of 73) is more than half, and the ten ARCTIC events are not all finger-adding gains above 25 %.
The correlation is not zero even for the spatial class on TACO, and it is 0.40 / 0.52 for the mixed class: do not write 'contact-change size is unrelated to capability change'.
entries.claim_as_extracted: The size of the dense contact-map change is only weakly associated with the capability change for persistent spatial events on TACO (Spearman 0.19 with the relative change, −0.27 with the retention, n = 119) and moderately on ARCTIC (0.55 / −0.60, n = 26), which is consistent with a large dense contact change providing little information about a capability change on TACO, while on ARCTIC the large-change spatial events mostly do change the capability.
entries.correction_reason: Correlations and quadrant values are exact. 'Mostly do change the capability' is true only against the strict train-median cut (10 of 11 exceed |0.09|); against the ±25 % band used everywhere else on the page it is 5 of 11, so the criterion has to be stated. The ARCTIC statement rests on 11 events and the Spearman values have no interval or p-value in the source.

entries.claim: The persistent spatial result is stable across ten modelling settings (the primary one and nine one-at-a-time changes of friction, patch merging, contact threshold and force-budget scheme): the median pre→post retention stays between 0.82 and 0.92 on TACO and between 0.76 and 0.94 on ARCTIC, and the median relative change between 0.00 and +0.04 (TACO) and −0.01 and +0.04 (ARCTIC). The largest shifts are the 0.5 cm contact threshold on ARCTIC (retention 0.76 [0.71, 0.81] against 0.89) and the single whole-hand budget, which raises retention to 0.92 (TACO) and 0.94 (ARCTIC). All settings stay inside the same contact-patch model.

These tables use 123 (TACO) / 26 (ARCTIC) events.

caveats: The sensitivity tables are computed over 123 TACO persistent spatial events (the 4 not firm throughout are included) and over 452 / 131 persistent mixed events although the report labels the mixed rows 'firm throughout'; their 'primary' row therefore differs slightly from Table 1 (TACO spatial relative change 0.0322 [0.0011, 0.0585] versus 0.0362 [0.0037, 0.0761]). One setting is varied at a time and all settings stay inside the same model family; this is not robustness to real physics (no mass, inertia or force limits).
The ARCTIC dip at the 0.5 cm threshold (0.76 [0.71, 0.81]) must stay visible; the report explains it by grasps losing contacts on one side, which is an explanation, not a tested result.

The report's statement that the mixed class 'stays clearly above the spatial class in every setting' holds for the medians; with a single whole-hand budget the classes move close (TACO mixed 0.0424 versus spatial 0.0149; ARCTIC mixed 0.0542 [0.00, 0.13] versus spatial −0.0105 [−0.06, 0.08]).
entries.claim_as_extracted: The persistent spatial result is stable across the ten modelling settings that were varied one at a time: the median pre→post retention stays between 0.76 and 0.94 and the median relative change between −0.01 and +0.04 on both datasets, with the 0.5 cm contact threshold on ARCTIC (retention 0.76) as the one setting that moves a number noticeably.
entries.correction_reason: Ranges verified from the three sensitivity CSVs (TACO 0.8250-0.9219, ARCTIC 0.7640-0.9433; relative change TACO 0.0-0.0402, ARCTIC -0.0105-0.0410). Two wording problems: there are nine variations plus the primary setting, not ten variations; and 'the one setting that moves a number noticeably' is too strong, because the whole-hand budget moves TACO retention to 0.92 [0.90, 0.93], above the primary interval [0.81, 0.88]. Per-dataset ranges should be shown rather than one union range. Caveat: the TACO sensitivity rows use 123 events, 4 of them with no contact patch at either frame (relative change exactly 0, retention undefined).

entries.claim: Along the direction of the object's velocity change over the 8 frames after the event start (a force direction; no required wrench is computed), the grasp after a persistent spatial event is not systematically more capable than the grasp before it, transported to the same frame (median post / pre capacity ratio 1.06 [0.98, 1.14] on TACO; 0.94 [0.48, 0.98] on ARCTIC, i.e. slightly below 1), whereas persistent mixed events have ratios of 1.13–1.30 over the force, torque and support directions (8- and 16-frame horizons) with intervals above 1 on both datasets.
entries.metric: Report's 'Metric B': support-function capacity along three observable directions of the object's future motion — change of translational velocity over K = 8 or 16 frames after the event start (a pure force), change of angular velocity (a pure torque), and world-up (support against gravity). Directions only: no required wrench is computed because mass and inertia are unknown. Here the PRE grasp IS transported to the POST frame (patches kept on their mesh vertex ids; ARCTIC's lid follows the articulation). Ratio = post / pre capacity, median over events, 95 % take-bootstrap CI; 1 = no change, above 1 = POST grasp more capable along that direction.

caveats: Direction-only analysis: it uses normalised directions of the object's kinematics, never a required wrench; ARCTIC's hinge torque is not turned into a direction, and low-motion windows give noisy directions (report section 12).

On ARCTIC the force ratio at K = 8 is below 1 with an interval that excludes 1 ([0.48, 0.98]): the post grasp is slightly less able along that direction. The report's summary phrase 'intervals including 1' is therefore not exact for this cell.
This supports 'not better aligned with the coming motion under the model'; it is not evidence about human intent and not a null-space measurement (no Jacobian null space was computed).
entries.claim_as_extracted: Along the directions in which the object is about to move, the grasp after a persistent spatial event is not systematically more capable than the grasp before it (post / pre capacity ratio for the force direction over the next 8 frames: 1.06 [0.98, 1.14] on TACO, 0.94 [0.48, 0.98] on ARCTIC), whereas persistent mixed events have ratios of 1.13–1.30 with intervals above 1 on both datasets.
entries.correction_reason: Values match the table. Two precision points: the direction is that of the change of translational velocity over K frames after the event START (an acceleration direction), not the direction of motion; and the upper end 1.30 comes from the 16-frame horizon on ARCTIC (1.2956 [1.09, 1.57] force, 1.2976 [1.02, 1.62] torque), which the entry's number list does not contain (verified in the CSV). This is the one measure where the pre grasp is transported by mesh vertex id. Direction-only analysis; no intent or null-space reading.

dataset_differences: Sample size: TACO 119 persistent spatial events from 73 takes, ARCTIC 26 from 15. ARCTIC intervals are much wider (retention [0.76, 0.96] versus [0.81, 0.88]; cosine [0.91, 0.99] versus [0.96, 0.97]).

Median relative change of the capability: TACO +0.036 with an interval just above zero [0.004, 0.076] (small but systematic gain; mean +0.13 [0.07, 0.21]; Q_post > Q_pre in 63 % of events); ARCTIC +0.021 with an interval straddling zero [−0.09, +0.19] (mean +0.05 [−0.11, +0.21]; 54 %).
Contact-change size versus capability change (persistent spatial): weak on TACO (Spearman 0.19 with the relative change, −0.27 with retention), moderate on ARCTIC (0.55, −0.60; n = 26).

Large-contact-change spatial events: on TACO 33 of 73 (45 % [34, 57]) keep |relative change| below the train median; on ARCTIC only 1 of 11 (9 % [0, 30]). The report's own wording for ARCTIC: 'the typical spatial event is wrench-neutral, the large ones are mostly not'.
Retention by number of reconfigured hand parts (persistent spatial): monotone on TACO (0.89 / 0.84 / 0.80; n = 29 / 31 / 59), flat on ARCTIC (0.90 / 0.91 / 0.88; n = 5 / 6 / 15).

Finger behaviour in persistent spatial events: TACO 1.13 parts slide, 0.50 appear, 0.24 disappear per event, 4.2 → 4.4 parts touching; ARCTIC 1.54 slide, 0.27 appear, 0.27 disappear, 3.4 → 3.4 parts touching.
Sensitivity to the contact threshold: at 0.5 cm TACO retention is unchanged (0.858) while ARCTIC drops to 0.764 [0.707, 0.812]; this is the only setting that moves a number noticeably.
Future-motion directions (persistent spatial, force direction, K = 8): TACO post/pre ratio 1.06 [0.98, 1.14]; ARCTIC 0.94 [0.48, 0.98], i.e. below 1 with an interval excluding 1.
Strict single-hand measure: retention 0.66 [0.33, 0.78] on TACO, 0.75 [0.11, 0.92] on ARCTIC; the single hand covers 0.41 → 0.50 of the 76 directions exactly on TACO but only 0.22 → 0.20 on ARCTIC.
Amount-dominant (diagnostic) class: median relative change +0.73 [0.24, 0.92] on TACO versus +0.14 [0.00, 0.95] on ARCTIC; retention 0.54 versus 0.62.
Persistent mixed class is similar on both datasets (median relative change +0.19 / +0.16; retention 0.76 / 0.75; 46 % / 46 % gain more than 25 %), with a much wider ARCTIC interval ([0.05, 0.45]).
Transient reference class: TACO is a random subsample of 150 of 708 events (retention 0.90); ARCTIC has all 12 events (0.94).
Event length: PRE and POST frames are 1 frame apart in the median TACO event and 2 in the median ARCTIC event.

Objects: TACO is rigid tool use (the tool also touches a target object); ARCTIC objects are articulated (the lid is rotated by the articulation angle). Both are bimanual and only one hand is modelled at a time.
OakInk2 is not part of this study (no hand geometry in the object frame in its caches); every F1-D statement is for TACO and ARCTIC only.
do_not_claim: 'Spatial contact changes do not matter' or 'all spatial reconfigurations are function-preserving': the result is a median over one event class; 20 % (TACO) / 23 % (ARCTIC) of persistent spatial events gain more than 25 % capability and 8 / 3 events lose more than 25 %.
'Null-space motion' or 'the fingers move in the grasp's null space': no Jacobian or grasp-map null space was measured; the report speaks only of redundancy 'under the modelled wrench constraints'.

'Function-preserving' without the qualifier 'modelled wrench capability' / 'under the modelled constraints': there is no mass, centre of mass, inertia, force limit or friction measurement; it is not a physical feasibility result.
Anything about human intent, comfort, fatigue, slip correction or purposelessness: the report explicitly excludes motive inference; wrench capability is a proxy for functional grasp capability.
'The grasp before retains 85–90 % of the capability in every direction' (the report's own loose phrase): retention is a mean over 76 directions of a capped ratio, and it is one-sided.

'The grasps before and after are equivalent because retention is about 0.85–0.89': retention is one-sided (a shrunken grasp scores about 1); report the reverse retention, cosine or relative change alongside.
'Release preserves capability (retention 1.0)' or 'onset changes capability by a factor of 1e9': both are artifacts (one-sided definition; division by epsilon when Q_pre = 0).
'Retention and cosine are computed after transporting the pre grasp by vertex id': transport is used only for the future-motion directions.
'Persistent mixed events always change capability': about half stay within ±25 % (49 % / 43 %).
'On ARCTIC, large spatial contact changes preserve capability': only 1 of 11 large-change events stays below the train-median change.

The report's sentence 'on ARCTIC these functional regrasps are most of the large-contact-change spatial events (10 of 11), on TACO fewer than half (55 %)': 55 % is more than half and the ten ARCTIC events are not all finger-adding gains above 25 %.
The report's '0.5–2.7 fingers appearing' in the events that gain more than 25 %: not reproduced by events.csv (mean 1.46, range 0–4, on TACO; exactly 1 on ARCTIC).

'Contact-change size is unrelated to capability change': Spearman is 0.19 on TACO but 0.55 on ARCTIC for spatial events, and 0.40 / 0.52 for mixed events; no intervals are given for these correlations.

'Finger additions cause the capability gain' as an established causal result: it is an association in observational data, and with one unit budget per finger an added finger raises the modelled capability by construction of the model.

'Finger removals lower capability' as a report finding: the report discusses additions; the removal pattern (8 of 8 and 3 of 3 loss events have a part disappearing) is a count made from events.csv in this pass.
A pooled number such as '145 events' or a retention averaged over TACO and ARCTIC: the datasets are never pooled.
'The result holds on OakInk2' or 'on all three datasets': OakInk2 was excluded.
'Robust to the physics': the ten sensitivity settings stay inside the same contact-patch model; under the strict single-hand measure retention is 0.66 / 0.75.

'A deterministic contact model cannot predict these events' as a result of this study: it is the report's interpretation; this study measured no prediction error. The word 'missed' rests on the hand-contact predictive-information report ('least explained').

'The Figure F examples are typical': they are selected extremes (highest retention, largest gain among events with an above-median contact change); three of the four 'equivalent' examples actually lost capability (−0.10, −0.17, −0.13).

'Contact does not move over time' or 'post-grasp reconfigurations are rare': persistent spatial events are 123 of 1 464 detected TACO test events and 26 of 283 on ARCTIC, alongside 452 / 131 persistent mixed events that more often change capability.
'The post grasp is never better aligned with the coming motion': true for the spatial class under the direction-only analysis, but the mixed class has ratios of 1.13–1.30 with intervals above 1.

'119 events from 177 takes' or 'the test split has 177 / 37 takes': the events come from 73 / 15 takes, and the fixed test split has 186 / 44 takes (177 / 37 are the takes with at least one detected event).
Units such as newtons or newton-metres for the capability: values are normalised (finger budget = 1, torque divided by the object's largest vertex radius).

attached_by_the_verifier: A table by finger-set change for the persistent spatial class, which the block asks for and the extractor gave only as scattered counts. Row counts over reports/wrench_counterfactual/events.csv made in this verification pass (not printed in the report, no intervals): TACO same set 62 (within ±25 %: 61, gain > 25 %: 1, loss > 25 %: 0); part added 45 (20 / 23 / 2; 12 of the 45 also lost a part); part removed only 12 (6 / 0 / 6). ARCTIC same set 15 (15 / 0 / 0); part added 7 (1 / 6 / 0; 1 also lost a part); part removed only 4 (1 / 0 / 3). Totals reproduce the table shares (87 / 24 / 8 of 119; 17 / 6 / 3 of 26).

Direct evidence for 'sliding in place' is not in the extractor output: among same-set events, the slide-only ones (at least one part moved more than 1 cm, none added or removed) are 33 on TACO (32 within ±25 %) and 10 on ARCTIC (10 within ±25 %); events.csv count from this pass. The report's Table 5 split cannot show this because it counts slid parts as reconfigured.

Sensitivity caveat to sharpen: the 4 extra TACO events in the sensitivity tables (123 instead of 119) have no contact patch at either frame (Q_pre = Q_post = 0, relative change exactly 0, retention undefined and dropped, cosine 0). That is why the retention median and interval equal Table 1 while the relative-change and cosine medians are pulled towards 0.

Report prose slips the page must not copy (table / CSV values are the right ones): section 9 gives TACO retention at mu 0.3 as 0.83 (CSV 0.8250, Table 4a 0.82) and ARCTIC retention at mu 1.0 as 0.92 (CSV 0.9145, Table 4a 0.91); section 7 gives the ARCTIC persistent mixed retention interval as [0.67, 0.81] (CSV 0.6647, Table 1 0.66). Already flagged by the extractor and confirmed: Limitations '100 events ... 61 takes' and '(37 takes)'; final answer '10 of 11 ... fewer than half (55 %)'; '0.5-2.7 fingers appearing' (events.csv: mean 1.46, range 0-4 on TACO; exactly 1 on ARCTIC).

No interval or test exists for the class contrasts the block leans on: the shares (within ±25 %, gain > 25 %), the Table-5 medians, the finger-set counts and the Spearman correlations all come without intervals. 'More often' is a descriptive comparison of shares and should be worded that way.

Locator correction for the word 'missed' in the block title: the phrase 'least explained' is in the wrench report's own section 2 (line 44), summarising the earlier study; hand_contact_predictive_info_report.md lines 24-26 give the numbers (ARCTIC persistent spatial +1.6 % n.s. at k = 8, oracle -8 %; TACO -4 % / -6 %, oracle -25 %) without that phrase. This unit measures no prediction error, so 'missed' needs the evidence of the hand-information unit beside it.

Block title wording: 'function-preserving' has to carry the qualifier 'modelled wrench capability' (a proxy in normalised units, single-hand support-function measure); under the strict exact-direction measure the median retention is 0.66 [0.33, 0.78] (TACO) / 0.75 [0.11, 0.92] (ARCTIC).

Retention detail missing from the metric description: the mean runs only over the directions in which at least one of the two grasps has capacity (> 1e-6), with 1e-6 added to the denominator (wrench_lp.py retention()).
